description.narrative: The PDO is to lower transport costs, improve accessibility and road safety, and support job creation along selected regional corridors.

The proposed project will finance specific activities from the following two IPF operations i.e. (1) Uganda North-Eastern Road Corridor Asset Management Project (NERAMP) (P125590) which closed on December 31, 2025 – see Component 1 below, and (2) Uganda: Roads and Bridges in the Refugee Hosting Districts/Koboko-Yumbe-Moyo Road Corridor Project (P171339) – see Components 2 and 3 below. 1) The Northeastern Road-corridor Asset Management Project (NERAMP) in Uganda was established to minimize transport costs, improve road safety, and maintain and enhance road assets through a comprehensive, multi-year infrastructure program. This initiative focuses on the sustainable management and rehabilitation of the key 340 km Tororo–Mbale–Soroti–Lira–Kamdini corridor, which serves as an essential international route linking the Port of Mombasa (Kenya) with South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo via Uganda. The project was divided into two primary sections: Lot 1 (Tororo-Mbale-Soroti, 150.8 km) and Lot 2 (Soroti-Lira-Kamdini, 189.4 km). Due to necessary scope adjustments aimed at ensuring value for money, the original financing was sufficient only for Lot 2 and a small segment of Lot 1, subsequently restructured and renamed Lot 1A. The remaining unfunded portion, designated Lot 1B, is now addressed as component 1 under this project. 2) The Roads and Bridges in the Refugee Hosting Districts/Koboko-Yumbe-Moyo Road Corridor Project is a significant infrastructure program funded by the World Bank. Its goal is to upgrade roads across northern Uganda's refugee-hosting districts, which will improve transportation for both refugees and local residents. The project is scheduled to close in 2027. The initiative focuses on better transport links, supporting livelihoods, and carefully managing social and environmental impacts. Specifically, the project aims to improve road connectivity, streamline supply deliveries for refugees and host communities, and strengthen the Ministry of Works and Transport's management of environmental and social risks. It includes upgrading the 103-kilometer Koboko-Yumbe-Moyo (KYM) road corridor in Uganda's West Nile Sub-region. At its core, the KYM Project is a key development effort to connect vital areas, enhance infrastructure, and support the large populations of refugees and their hosts in Northern Uganda. After a request from the Government of Uganda for further assistance, additional measures have been introduced: rehabilitating 16 km of town roads and 15 km of access roads in Koboko, Yumbe, and Moyo districts, along with climate-resilient roadside rest areas, weighbridge, and markets construction in each district. These new interventions are now included as components 2 and 3 of this project.Component 1: Climate resilient upgrading of highway corridors - Road rehabilitation, operations and maintenance including institutional support (estimated cost: US$146 million). Activities finance under this component includes the rehabilitation and maintenance of the remaining 150.8 km section of the Tororo - Mbale - Soroti road section, road safety interventions and support to enhance road asset management system. The component will also finance capacity building for managing OPRC contracts and hands-on training for newly graduated interns. These activities will build on and complement the initial NERAMP project activities. (a) Subcomponent 1.1: Design, Road rehabilitation, performance maintenance and weigh bridge operations (US$128 million): This subcomponent will finance the civil works on the remainder of the Tororo - Mbale- Soroti road (150.8 km) (US$ 128 million) including the dual weighbridge at km 46+700 in Mbale. Out of the US$ 128 million, the rehabilitation and upgrading of the Tororo-Mbale-Soroti road section to climate resilience standards will strengthen the reliability of the road corridor link between South Sudan, parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and northern and eastern Uganda to the port of Mombasa strengthening the resilience of the transport network. The works and services attributed to the US$ 128 million will include: (1) the design and rehabilitation of sections of the road corridor to climate resilient standards including the use of engineering and nature-based solutions to address current and projected extreme rainfall and flood events, rising temperatures and drought conditions (US$112.2 million); (2) routine and periodic maintenance of the whole corridor in light of climate risks and hotspots (US$14.8 million); (3) activities such as management of traffic, road safety, climate risk preparedness and response and axle load control measures i.e. weigh bridge operations (US$1 million). (b) Subcomponent 1.2: Institutional support through the upgrade of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS), the upgrade of the Traffic Management System (TMS) and mainstream Road Safety Activities (US$5.5 million). The subcomponent will finance (i) A Road Asset Management System and procedures by main streaming climate resilience in the lifecycle of transport asset management (US$ 1 million); (ii) Road safety activities (US$ 2.5 million) and upgrade of the Traffic Management System (TMS) (US$2.0 million). The Traffic Management Systems (TMS) will optimize the road network by utilizing real-time data to monitor traffic and reduce congestion. Key activities under the TMS shall include adaptive signal timing, incident detection and response coordination, ramp metering, dynamic lane/speed management, vehicle/pedestrian tracking, and providing traveler information i.e., (i) Real-Time Monitoring: Using sensors and cameras to monitor traffic conditions and identify issues on highways; (ii) Active Traffic Control: Adjusting traffic signals based on demand, managing ramp meters, and controlling reversible lanes to optimize flow; (iii) Incident Management: Coordinating with law enforcement and emergency services to detect crashes, manage traffic scenes, and clear incidents to restore capacity; (iv) Demand & Flow Management: Implementing dynamic lane use control, variable speed limits, and managing queues to prevent bottlenecks; (v) Information Dissemination: Providing real-time updates to travelers regarding congestion, weather conditions, and travel times; (vi) Data Analysis & Planning: Analyzing historical and real-time data to improve future traffic strategies.The NERAMP parent project prioritized road safety interventions like driver/school sensitization, signage, and enforcement along the Tororo-Kamdini corridor, aiming to reduce accidents, though implementation faced challenges requiring corrective actions and focus on proper road guidance (signage, enforcement) for drivers. This project will enhance road safety by implementing a Safe Systems Approach, which integrates improved infrastructure elements such as walkways, lighting, and bridges, alongside strengthened management of the road network. The Safe System Approach is designed to account for human error and lessen crash severity, with the goal of achieving zero fatalities. Key initiatives include upgrading roundabouts at intersections, constructing separated pedestrian walkways in peri-urban areas, reducing speed limits through the installation of speed humps, and improving intersections with curb extensions to protect vulnerable road users. These activities collectively aim to reduce road traffic injuries and fatalities by building robust road safety management capacity. (c) Subcomponent 1.3: Institutional support through a capacity building program (US$2.5 million). This subcomponent will finance (i) Technical Assistance (TA) to strengthen MoWT's capacity for Design, Procurement, Management and Supervision of contracts including not limited to HDM licensing and training (US$1 million) and (ii) a capacity building program on climate resilient asset management including a gender focused training programme for young professionals to build experience towards providing support
